new_statements.quote: (Bukharan Tajik phonology, unlike the Turkish one, does not assign stress to the last syllable in a domain of stressing rules [...]) The postposition/suffix -ba is usually unstressed in Bukharan Tajik (which is also the case with its standard Tajik equivalent, preposition ba) as can be seen in the following domains of the operation of stressing rules: xoná-ba [house-to] (Rastorgueva 1964:115) čūčqá-ba [pig-to] bozór-ba [market-to] Regrettably, there is not an extensive study of the phonology of Bukharan Tajik. We are therefore reluctant to call the apparently consistent lack of stress on -ba an established phonological ‘rule’.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog has no record and no existing statement for bukh1238, so there is nothing to agree with or contradict; this is the first first-hand placement statement held by the project for the language. Caveats: (a) the open_url does not lead to the LINCOM 2007 grammar sketch but to Ido's 2001 Sydney PhD thesis on incomplete sentences in agglutinative languages, a different work (wrong item), which was nevertheless read in full; (b) it describes Bukharan Tajik as spoken by young Bukharans generally, not specifically the Jewish variety that bukh1238 denotes; (c) it gives three noun examples and refuses to call the pattern a rule. The live URL could not be reached by automated download twice (…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the last syllable of the stem (xoná, čūčqá, bozór); the postposition/suffix -ba (like the literary-Tajik preposition ba, one of the 'words and morphemes without stress' of Rustamov & Ghafforov 1985:56, cited in fn. 130) lies outside the stress domain, so the larger domain stem+-ba is not final-stressed. The author explicitly declines to call this an established rule and says no extensive phonology of Bukharan Tajik exists. Sentence-level prominence can be shifted onto -ba by information structure (čūčqa-BA gap zadani man), which the thesis treats as sentence prominence, not word stress. Alternative label: fixed: other position (stem-final with extrametrical enclitic).
new_statements.exceptions: Postposition/suffix -ba is unstressed; the thesis refers (fn. 130) to a class of unstressed words and morphemes in literary Tajik (Rustamov & Ghafforov 1985:56) but lists no others for Bukharan Tajik. Informants split 2 vs 4 on whether information-structural prominence may override the -ba stress pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Ido's data are 'Bukharan Tajik', the Tajik dialect of the city of Bukhara, taken largely from young Bukharans in their twenties with no formal education in standard Tajik (thesis, Notes on the Text and section 1.2.3.3.4.2, p. 36); the religious affiliation of the informants is not stated, so the statement is not first-hand for the Jewish variety (Bukharic/Judeo-Tajik, ISO bhh) that bukh1238 denotes. Glottolog itself files Ido's Bukharan Tajik works under bukh1238, and Ido 2017 (JJL 5:83) reports that Jewish Bukharan Tajik speakers are not perceived as having a discernible accent relative to other Bukharan Tajik speakers, so the placement plausibly carries over, but it should be marked as a related-variety statement.

sources.citation: Ido, Shinji. 2017. The Vowel System of Jewish Bukharan Tajik: With Special Reference to the Tajik Vowel Chain Shift. Journal of Jewish Languages 5(1): 81-103. doi:10.1163/22134638-12340078 (CC-BY-NC open access; Nagoya University repository copy)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Vowel system only; no statement on word stress of Jewish Bukharan Tajik (the word 'stress' occurs once, about Modern Hebrew). Identity-relevant: 'nor do Jewish residents of Bukhara appear to be perceived by their fellow townsmen, namely Bukharan Tajik speakers, as having a discernible accent, let alone a distinct dialect or language' (p. 82); notes Samarkand Jewish Tajik differs from Bukharan Jewish Tajik (Zarubin 1928; Ešniëzov 1977: 65).

sources.citation: Ido, Shinji. 2014. Bukharan Tajik (Illustrations of the IPA). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 44(1): 87-102. doi:10.1017/S002510031300011X
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No stress/accent section (sections are Consonants, Vowels, Vowel length, Intonation, Transcription). Only incidental stress marks in the vowel-reduction paragraph, p. 91: /beˈɾaXm/ 'merciless', /biˈɾinʥ/ 'rice' (final stress in these two words), with no rule stated. Describes Bukharan Tajik generally (the city dialect that standard Tajik was based on), not the Jewish variety specifically; says it 'differs little from standard Tajik phonologically and phonetically' (p. 87).

sources.note: 'From a phonological and prosodic perspective, Judeo-Tajik is distinguished by a number of different question and exclamation intonations, as well as by the existence of unique phonemes (the guttural Hebrew letters het and ayin).' No word-stress statement. Bibliography lists Zarubin 1928, Babaev 1934, Birnbaum 1950, Niyazov 1979, Rastorgueva 1963/1964 etc.
